title: Aleatoric vs Epistemic Uncertainty
description: Der Kiureghian and Ditlevsen's distinction: aleatoric uncertainty is the world's randomness (more data won't remove it); epistemic is our ignorance (more data will). The quantifier labels every uncertainty — the remedies differ.

demo.code:
import random, math, statistics
random.seed(1001)
n=2000
# Monte Carlo propagation: y = x1^2 + x2, x1~N(2,0.5), x2~N(0,1)
xs1=[random.gauss(2,0.5) for _ in range(n)]
xs2=[random.gauss(0,1) for _ in range(n)]
ys=[a*a+b for a,b in zip(xs1,xs2)]
mean=statistics.mean(ys); sd=statistics.stdev(ys)
srt=sorted(ys); lo=srt[int(0.025*n)]; hi=srt[int(0.975*n)]
# analytic check: E[x1^2]=Var+mean^2=0.25+4=4.25, E[y]=4.25
print(f"n=2000 mean={mean:.3f} (analytic 4.250) sd={sd:.3f}")
print(f"95% interval=[{lo:.3f},{hi:.3f}] contains_analytic={'yes' if lo<4.25<hi else 'NO'}")
print("DEMO_OK")
demo.output:
n=2000 mean=4.228 (analytic 4.250) sd=2.279
95% interval=[0.380,9.344] contains_analytic=yes
DEMO_OK
demo.note: Runnable demo program verified by execution during the database build.

architecture: Uncertainties are classified by source; aleatoric components get distributions, epistemic get learning plans. The label travels with every number.
